17.t: Working with data: pulse and exercise
q: Calculate the percentage increase in the untrained student’s pulse from rest to the end of exercise.
Compare the recovery of the two students.
The athlete’s pulse falls faster and is back to resting by about 8–10 min; the untrained student is still 2 beats above resting at 10 min. The athlete also has a lower resting and peak rate.
Explain why the pulse rate rises during exercise.
Muscles respire faster, so they need more oxygen and glucose and must lose more CO₂. Rising CO₂ is detected and the medulla speeds up the sinoatrial node.
The athlete’s resting pulse is lower, yet the same amount of blood is pumped per minute at rest. Explain.
A larger, stronger ventricle pumps more blood per beat (stroke volume), so fewer beats give the same output.
Suggest why the pulse stays above resting for several minutes after exercise stops.
Lactate must be oxidised and extra CO₂ removed (oxygen debt), and the body is still warm, so extra oxygen is still needed.
A positive correlation: more saturated fat, more CHD deaths. One country (15%, 90 deaths) does not fit the pattern.
Use the line to estimate the death rate expected at 10% saturated fat.
Suggest two reasons why the country at 15% has far fewer deaths than the line predicts.
Any two: other parts of the diet (olive oil, fish, vegetables); less smoking; more exercise; a younger population; deaths recorded differently.
Explain why these data do not show that saturated fat causes CHD.
They show only a correlation. Other variables such as smoking, exercise, wealth and age are not controlled, and the data are national averages, not individuals.
Outline a study that would give stronger evidence of a causal link.

A large randomised controlled trial: people randomly given low or high saturated fat diets, other factors kept similar, CHD followed for years (or a long cohort study that adjusts for smoking, age and exercise).
